newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraqi paper wants U.N. arms inspector's dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Iraqi paper wants U.N. arms inspector's dismissal.

text.p: The newspaper of President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday called on Tuesday for the dismissal of the U.N.'s chief weapons inspector for Iraq, saying it expected nothing but lies from his next trip to Baghdad.
Rolf Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM) on Iraq, is due in Baghdad on Thursday for talks with Iraqi leaders to defuse a U.N.-Iraq standoff over long-range missiles.

"The world public opinion...should call for the sacking of Ekeus because his targets, known and clear, are for the obstruction of any possible chance to lift the embargo on Iraq," the paper Babel said in a front-page editorial.
"The new trip by Ekeus will be shrouded with new lies and expected fabrications," it added.

Sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait can be lifted only when Ekeus's commission decides that Iraq has scrapped all its weapons of mass destruction, including missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).
Babel accused Ekeus of turning his commission into an agency to further U.S. interests rathern than implementating U.N. ceasefire resolutions which ended the 1991 Gulf War over Kuwait.

It also lambasted U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, saying she and Ekeus were trying to prolong sanctions on Iraq and scupper Baghdad's oil-for-food deal with the U.N. aimed at alleviating the impact of international sanctions.

The attack by Babel was the second in Iraq's press on Ekeus in seven days. The official al-Iraq newspaper last week accused the envoy of "aggressive remarks" and attempts to escalate tension with Iraq.

Iraq and the United Nations are locked in dispute over the removal of some 100 wrecked missile engines for analysis to the United States. Iraq would like them to be examined in either Russia or France.
UNSCOM uncovered the missiles last year. It sent two more teams to Iraq this year to supervise further digs for missing missile parts.

Iraq says it has destroyed all its banned missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles) but UNSCOM doubts the authenticity of the engines unearthed. The analysis in the United States, it adds, is necessary to determine if they were the engines known to have been imported from the former Soviet Union or manufactured domestically.
Babel said Ekeus's insistence that Iraq was still hiding banned missiles was a game and he lose his job "because of his bias and animosity towards Iraq".
It said Ekeus with U.S. assistance was waging a war against Iraq which it likened to the one launched by the United States and its allies in 1991 to eject Iraqi troops from Kuwait.
